system:
You are an experienced litigator who has supervised many document reviews. You
are asked to estimate, item by item, how hard it is for a human reviewer to
check one call, and to say why.

### The reviewer's task

The reviewer is law-trained but not a specialist in the case's industry, and
**has already read and understood this case**: the opinion, the contracts, and
every court defect — each provision the court construed, and for each one every
distinct defect the court construed in it, with the passage of the opinion it
comes from.

They are now given a list of **items**. Each item is one description of a
defect, written by someone else about one provision the court construed, and
the call a first reader made on it. The call is one of two kinds:

- **A match.** The first reader said the description names one particular court
  defect on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether it does — whether
  the description and that court defect are about the same words and the same
  problem with them — and not some other court defect, or none.
- **No match.** The first reader said the description names none of the court
  defects on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether that is right —
  whether the description fails to name each one of them.

You are judging **how hard it is to reach that decision** for each item. Not
whether the first reader was right: do not decide that, and do not let a view
on it set the difficulty. Not how hard the case is: the reviewer already knows
the case, so count only the work this item adds.

### What does not count

- **How hard the case is.** Two items in one case can differ widely. Rate each
  item by what checking it takes on top of an understanding of the case.
- **The number of items.** Each item is rated on its own, and an item does not
  get easier or harder because there are many others.
- **Length by itself.** A long description is hard only where its length makes
  it unclear what it names.
- **How close the description is to the court defect.** A full match, a clear
  partial match and a clear mismatch are all easy to check. Difficulty is how
  hard it is to **see** how close they are, not how close they turn out to be.
- **Wording.** A description that calls the court's problem by another name —
  "indefinite" where the court said "ambiguous", "open-ended" where it said
  "unclear" — about the same words is no harder to check than one that uses
  the court's own word.
- **Distinctions the court did not draw.** Two framings of what is wrong with
  the same words — its meaning is uncertain, its reach is too broad — can be
  told apart in theory. A reviewer does not stop over that unless **the court's
  construction turned on it**: unless the court accepted one framing and
  rejected the other, or decided the case on a point one framing reaches and
  the other misses. Where the court did not, the reviewer sees the same words
  and the same kind of complaint, and confirms the call at a glance.

### How a reviewer actually checks an item

To check an item the reviewer has to settle, in turn:

1. **What the description is about** — which words, which other provision or
   document, and what it says is wrong with them;
2. **whether each thing it asserts is true** — what the contract says, what a
   term or a document is, what happened between the parties;
3. **whether that is what the court construed** — the same words, and the
   point the court's construction actually turned on;
4. **whether the call follows** — given all that, does the description name the
   matched court defect, or none of them.

An item is easy when every step is quick and the answer to each is plain. It is
hard when a step cannot be finished from the clause and the passage, or when,
with every step done, it is still not plain what the answer is.

### What makes an item easy to check

The comparison is clear-cut, whichever way it comes out:

- **One phrase, one step.** The description points at a phrase of the clause
  and says what is wrong with it in one step — this phrase is vague, this term
  is undefined — and the court construed that phrase for that reason. The
  reviewer reads the description once and confirms it against the passage.
- **Plainly different.** The description is about other words, or a different
  problem, so the mismatch is seen just as quickly.
- **Anything extra is plainly separate.** Where the description also raises a
  point about another clause, term or objection, that point is set aside at a
  glance; it does not need to be checked to decide the call.
- **Nothing to verify.** What the description asserts can be seen in the
  clause and the passage themselves.
- **The provision has one court defect**, or its court defects are clearly
  separate, so there is only one comparison to make.

An item like that takes a minute or two, and the reviewer ends confident.

### What makes an item hard to check

What makes an item hard is that **a step cannot be settled from the clause and
the passage, or the answer stays unclear once it is**. Each of these adds time,
and they compound:

- **The two sides may name the same thing differently.** The description
  refers to a document, a party, a transaction or a category of things by one
  name, and the court by another, and whether they are the same thing is a
  question of fact — about the deal, the record or the industry — that the
  reviewer has to look up before the comparison can even start.
- **The description makes claims that have to be verified.** It asserts facts
  about the contract, the parties, a court or a body, a document or the
  background, and the reviewer has to check them against the contract, the
  opinion or outside knowledge. Some may turn out to be wrong.
- **It bundles several claims about the same defect, some of them doubtful.**
  The description makes several points about the same words or the same
  dispute; some look right and some look wrong. The reviewer has to grade each
  and then decide whether the call stands on the right ones.
- **It has the right words but not the court's point.** The description is
  about the words the court construed, but misses, or misstates, a point the
  court's construction actually turned on — one the opinion relies on, not one
  a reader could merely imagine. The reviewer has to decide whether that still
  names the court defect, and even with every fact checked, careful reviewers
  can disagree.
- **Its reasoning runs over several steps.** The description reaches its defect
  through a chain — this term, read with that provision, given this fact — and
  the reviewer has to follow and test each link.
- **The defect is relational and the description has only part of it.** The
  court's defect lies in how this provision is read with another provision or
  with a separate document, and the description addresses only this one, or
  only one side of the relationship, so the reviewer has to decide how much of
  the relationship it must reach before it counts.
- **The description is vague or general.** It could be read as naming the court
  defect or as naming something near it, and the reviewer has to decide how
  much it must say before it counts.
- **Several court defects on the provision are close to one another**, so the
  description could name one, another, or more than one of them, and the
  reviewer has to tell them apart before they can check the call.

An item like that can take half an hour or more, and the reviewer may still be
unsure at the end.

### The scale

- **`difficulty`** — `easy`, `intermediate` or `hard`.
- **`score`** — an integer from 1 to 10, and use the whole range. 1–3 is easy:
  1–2 when the decision is plain at a glance, 3 when one more look is needed.
  4–6 is intermediate: a claim to verify or a framing to work through, but the
  answer is plain once that is done. 7–10 is hard: 9–10 when, with every claim
  checked, two careful reviewers could still decide it differently.
  `difficulty` and `score` must agree.
- **`estimated_minutes`** — your estimate of how long the reviewer needs to
  reach a decision on this item, given that they already understand the case.
  Count only the work this item adds.
instructions:
Work in this order.

1. **Read the court defects** in the task and the provisions they sit in, until
   you could say what each one is about in a sentence.
2. **Go through the items one at a time.** For each one, read the description,
   then the court defects on its provision, then the call, and walk the four
   steps a reviewer takes: what the description is about, whether what it
   asserts is true, whether that is what the court construed, whether the call
   follows. Note which step takes work, what that work needs — the clause, the
   rest of the contract, the opinion, outside facts — and whether its answer is
   plain once the work is done.
3. **Rate the item by how clear that comparison is** — not by how close the
   description turns out to be, not by how hard the case is, and not by whether
   you think the call is right.

Return exactly one entry per item, under its id, in the order given.

In each `reason`, give one or two sentences specific to this item: name the
step that takes the work, and the words, claim or court defect it turns on.
task:
### The court defects in 814 F.Supp.2d 930

### Contract 814FSupp2d930_workout_agreement

#### c010 — Workout Arrangement Recital

```
WHEREAS, Customer has requested and Lender has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage pursuant to a loan work-out arrangement on the terms set forth herein.
```

- **d01** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): The recital that Aurora “has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage” created whole-contract tension with Attachment A’s statement that the Plan payments would be insufficient to pay the arrearage, leaving Aurora’s repayment obligation ambiguous when the agreement was read as a whole.
  Opinion lines 52-54:
```
In her second cause of action for breach of contract, Plaintiff alleges that “[Aurora] breached its contract with Plaintiff and the Class by failing to allow Plaintiff and the Class to repay their remaining arrearage, and by initiating foreclosure without notice and without an opportunity to cure despite its promise of providing access to a cure method.” FAC ¶ 66. As support for this claim, the FAC cites one of the recitals to the Workout Agreement, which expressly acknowledges that “Customer has requested and Lender has agreed to alloiv Customer to repay the Arrearage pursuant to a loan work-out arrangement on the terms set forth herein.” FAC Ex. A at 2, Bates No. AURORA 000151 (emphasis added). In response, Aurora points out that the Workout Agreement is subject to the terms set forth in Attachment A to the agreement, which states that the payment plan, in fact, “will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage” and that “[a]t the Expiration Date, a portion of the Arrearage will still be outstanding.” FAC Ex. A, Attachment A ¶ b, Bates No. AURORA 000148. Thus, according to Aurora, it had no contractual obligation to allow Plaintiff to repay her arrearage.
Under California law, a contract must be interpreted in a manner that gives effect to the mutual intent of the parties if that intent can be ascertained. Cal. Civ.Code § 1636. The whole of a contract must be construed together in order “to give effect to every part, if reasonably practicable, each clause helping to interpret the other.” Id. § 1641. “Courts must interpret contractual language in a manner [that] gives force and effect to every provision, and not in a way [that] renders some clauses nugatory, inoperative or meaningless.” City of Atascadero v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc., 68 Cal.App.4th 445, 473, 80 Cal.Rptr.2d 329 (1998). “If the contract language is clear and explicit, it governs.” Foster-Gardner, Inc. v. National Union Fire Ins. Co., 18 Cal.4th 857, 868, 77 Cal.Rptr.2d 107, 959 P.2d 265 (1998) (internal quotations and citation omitted). On the other hand, “[i]f an instrument is capable of two different reasonable interpretations, the instrument is ambiguous.” Harvey v. The Landing Homeowners Ass’n, 162 Cal.App.4th 809, 817, 76 Cal.Rptr.3d 41 (2008).
Aurora contends that the only obligation it assumed under the Workout Agreement was to temporarily forebear from foreclosing on her Property. Such a determination cannot be made at this stage of the proceedings, however. Although it is true that Attachment A discloses that the “aggregate Plan payment will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage,” Aurora never reconciles this provision with the recital that Aurora “has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage pursuant to a loan work-out arrangement^]” Nor does Aurora explain the first clause in the Attachment, which specifies that the payment plan is being implemented “[f]or the purposes of repayment of the Arrearage^]” Id. Bates No. 000157. As set forth above, the Court is not at liberty to credit the provisions of the Workout Agreement that favor Aurora while ignoring those which do not. See Sunset Sec. Co. v. Coward-McCann, Inc., 47 Cal.2d 907, 911, 306 P.2d 777 (1957) (“It is beyond question that every provision of a contract should be examined to determine the meaning and intention of the parties.”) (emphasis added). Given the apparent ambiguity created by the ostensibly contradictory provisions of the Workout Agreement, the viability of Plaintiffs breach of contract claim is not amenable to resolution at this stage of the litigation. See Consul Ltd. v. Solide Enters., Inc., 802 F.2d 1143, 1149 (9th Cir.1986) (holding that district court erred in dismissing breach of contract claim where contract was ambiguous).
```

#### c013 — 3 Lenders Forbearance

```
3 Lenders Forbearance Lender shall forbear from exercising any or all of its rights and remedies now existing or arising during the term of this Agreement under the Loan Documents, provided there 1s no "Default", as such term is defined in paragraph 6
```

- **d02** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): Aurora’s reading of its promise to forbear as its only obligation could not be accepted without reconciling that provision with the agreement’s provisions stating that Aurora would allow repayment of the arrearage.
  Opinion lines 52-54:
  The same passage as d01 above.

#### c031 — Attachment A a.1 Stipulated Payments

```
al For purposes of repayment of the Arrearage, Customer shall pay a stipulated payment of $1625 00 (the "Pirst Plan payment"), on or before 11/18/2009 ‘Thereafter, Customer shall pay five (5) consecutive stipulated monthly payments each in the amount of $1625 00 on or before the 15th day of every month (each, a "Due Date"), commencing 12/15/2009 and continuing through and including 04/15/2010 (the "Second Plan payment, Thard Plan payment, Fourth Plan payment, Fifth Plan payment, and Sixth Plan payment”, respectively).
```

- **d03** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): The statement that the stipulated payment plan was implemented “[f]or the purposes of repayment of the Arrearage” created whole-contract tension with the provision declaring that those payments would be insufficient to pay the arrearage.
  Opinion lines 52-54:
  The same passage as d01 above.

#### c041 — Attachment A b Plan Payment Insufficiency

```
b The aggregate Plan payment will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage. At the Expiration Date, a portion of the Arrearage will st111 be outstanding. Because payment of the Plan payments will not cure the Arrearage, Customer's account will remain delinquent.
```

- **d04** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): The statement that the “aggregate Plan payment will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage” supported Aurora’s denial of any repayment obligation but created whole-contract tension with the recital and payment-purpose clause stating that the arrangement was for repayment of the arrearage.
  Opinion lines 52-54:
  The same passage as d01 above.


### The items to rate

#### a01

On `814FSupp2d930_workout_agreement` c010 — Workout Arrangement Recital. Court defects on this provision: d01.

The description:
```
The recital that Lender "has agreed to allow Customer to repay the Arrearage" under the work-out arrangement conflicts with Attachment A paragraph b, which states the aggregate Plan payments will be insufficient to pay the Arrearage and that the account will remain delinquent. A borrower could argue the recital states the bargain's purpose and controls the operative payment schedule.
```

The first reader matched it to **d01**.

#### a02

On `814FSupp2d930_workout_agreement` c013 — 3 Lenders Forbearance. Court defects on this provision: d02.

The description:
```
"[F]orbear from exercising any or all of its rights and remedies" is ambiguous as to whether Lender must forbear from all remedies or may elect which ones to forbear from. The disjunctive "any or all" gives the borrower's principal protection no fixed content.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d02.

#### a03

On `814FSupp2d930_workout_agreement` c013 — 3 Lenders Forbearance. Court defects on this provision: d02.

The description:
```
The forbearance promise cannot be squared with paragraph 8, which states that a commenced foreclosure "will not be withdrawn," and with paragraph 7's declaration that nothing herein waives any right to commence or resume foreclosure. What Lender actually gave up during the plan term is the very thing those provisions take back.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d02.

#### a04

On `814FSupp2d930_workout_agreement` c031 — Attachment A a.1 Stipulated Payments. Court defects on this provision: d03.

The description:
```
The First Plan payment is due "on or before 11/18/2009," but the effectiveness condition in Attachment A requires Lender to receive that payment by the Agreement Return Date of 11/15/2009, and the cover letter demands it by 11/15/2009. A payment made on the date this provision allows would fail the condition another provision imposes.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d03.

#### a05

On `814FSupp2d930_workout_agreement` c041 — Attachment A b Plan Payment Insufficiency. Court defects on this provision: d04.

The description:
```
The statement that the aggregate Plan payments will be insufficient and the account will remain delinquent conflicts with the recital that Lender agreed to allow Customer "to repay the Arrearage pursuant to a loan work-out arrangement" and with paragraph 4's reference to full reinstatement. A court would have to decide what the plan was for if it could never cure the default.
```

The first reader matched it to **d04**.


### What to return

One entry per item above, each under its id.
